qs.q: A middle-aged patient presents with chronic skin lesions and a biopsy reveals a band-like lymphohistiocytic infiltrate at the dermo-epidermal junction with basal layer vacuolization. Direct immunofluorescence demonstrates granular IgG and complement deposition along the basement membrane zone. Which disease process is this?
o: Systemic lupus erythematosus manifesting characteristic interface dermatitis
Pemphigus vulgaris showing intraepidermal blister via desmoglein loss
Bullous pemphigoid displaying subepidermal separation with eosinophils
Dermatitis herpetiformis revealing granular IgA in dermal papillae
Psoriasis vulgaris exhibiting marked epidermal acanthosis and microabscesses
qs.e: Lupus band test and interface dermatitis features are classic for cutaneous manifestations of systemic lupus erythematosus.

qs.q: A renal biopsy from a patient with nephrotic syndrome shows diffuse thickening of the glomerular basement membrane. Silver staining reveals spike-and-dome patterns along the subepithelial space. Which underlying pathological mechanism is responsible?
o: Direct antibody-mediated destruction of podocyte foot processes
Subendothelial deposition of circulating cryoglobulins activating complement
In situ immune complex formation along subepithelial basement membrane
Deposition of monoclonal light chains forming organized fibrils
Accumulation of mesangial matrix causing global glomerulosclerosis
qs.e: Membranous nephropathy is characterized by subepithelial immune complex deposits creating a spike-and-dome pattern on silver stain.

qs.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with malar rash, arthralgia, and positive anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies. She develops diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis. Examination of her glomeruli using immunofluorescence microscopy reveals granular deposits along the basement membrane. These deposits consist primarily of:
o: Complement proteins activated exclusively by the alternative pathway
In situ autoantibodies directed against podocyte foot process proteins
Circulating antigen-antibody immune complexes trapped in capillary walls
T-cell receptor fragments shed during chronic local inflammation
Fibrinogen degradation products polymerizing within Bowman space
qs.e: Systemic lupus erythematosus nephritis is driven by the deposition of circulating immune complexes in glomerular capillary loops.

qs.q: A patient presents with hemoptysis, iron deficiency anemia, and pulmonary infiltrates. Renal function tests are completely normal, and anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies are absent. Which diagnosis best fits these findings?
qs.e: Idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis presents with pulmonary findings similar to Goodpasture syndrome but lacks renal disease and anti-GBM antibodies. Goodpasture syndrome is explicitly defined by the presence of renal disease and anti-GBM antibodies.

qs.q: Microscopic examination of a nasal polyp removed from an allergic patient reveals an oedematous stroma, eosinophilic infiltrate, thickened basement membrane, and which type of covering epithelium?
qs.e: Nasal polyps are benign lesions covered by respiratory ciliated columnar epithelium and lack malignant features. Stratified squamous epithelium lines sites subjected to mechanical friction like the oesophagus rather than nasal polyps.

qs.q: A 42-year-old man presents with acute kidney injury, nephritic urinary sediment, and pulmonary haemorrhage. Renal biopsy shows linear deposition of IgG along the glomerular basement membrane. Which of the following is the target antigen in this patient's condition?
o: the NC1 domain of type IV collagen
qs.e: This patient has Goodpasture syndrome, caused by anti-GBM antibodies targeting the NC1 domain of type IV collagen. PLA2R is the main target in primary membranous nephropathy.

qs.q: A renal biopsy shows thickened capillary walls on light microscopy, with electron microscopy revealing duplication of the basement membrane matrix in subendothelial locations. Which pathological response to glomerular injury does this represent?
qs.e: Basement membrane thickening can occur through deposition of electron-dense material, increased matrix synthesis, or duplication/additional layers of basement membrane matrix as seen in MPGN. It appears as thickened capillary walls on light microscopy.

qs.q: During the evaluation of a patient with a nephritic-nephrotic overlap syndrome, low serum C3 levels are found alongside normal C1 and C4 levels. Electron microscopy reveals dense, ribbon-like, osmiophilic deposits within the lamina densa of the glomerular basement membrane. What is the primary pathogenic driver of this condition?
o: Inherited mutations in the podocin gene disrupting the barrier
Deposition of circulating classical immune complexes containing IgG
Dysregulation of alternative complement pathway by C3 nephritic factor
Direct viral podocyte infection causing unselective filtration
qs.e: Dense deposit disease is caused by dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway, most commonly via C3 nephritic factor (an autoantibody stabilizing C3 convertase), leading to low C3 and normal C1/C4. Immune complex deposition involving the classical pathway typically results in depressed C1q and C4 in addition to C3.

es.q: What are the key differences distinguishing Idiopathic Pulmonary Hemosiderosis from Goodpasture syndrome? → Idiopathic Pulmonary Hemosiderosis has **no associated renal disease** and **no circulating anti-basement membrane antibody**, unlike Goodpasture syndrome.
es.m:
- **Renal sparing**: Idiopathic Pulmonary Hemosiderosis presents with pulmonary hemorrhage and iron-deficiency anemia completely without concurrent renal disease.
- **Antibody status**: Lacks the circulating anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) antibodies characteristic of Goodpasture syndrome.
- **Immunofluorescence**: Lung biopsy in idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis shows negative linear IgG deposition along the alveolar basement membranes.
- **Demographic difference**: Often affects children and young adults, whereas Goodpasture syndrome has a classic bimodal peak affecting young males and older adults.
- **Etiology**: The exact pathogenesis of idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis

ai.title: Basement Membrane Pathology
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: The basement membrane (BM) is a thin extracellular sheet that supports epithelia and endothelium. Damage or thickening of BM underlies key lung and kidney diseases, altering gas exchange and filtration. Recognising BM involvement guides diagnosis and targeted therapy.

sections.p: The basement membrane is a specialised extracellular matrix composed of type IV collagen, laminin, nidogen and proteoglycans. It separates epithelial or endothelial cells from underlying connective tissue and provides structural support and selective permeability.
b: In the lung it forms the alveolar‑capillary barrier with type I pneumocytes and capillary endothelium.
In the kidney it is the middle layer of the glomerular filtration barrier.

t.b: Confirms BM thickening or disruption; essential for diagnosing pulmonary fibrosis, Goodpasture syndrome, membranous nephropathy.
Detects circulating antibodies that target the glomerular BM; a positive result supports anti‑GBM disease.

sections.p: BM injury is staged by the extent of structural change and functional loss, often using disease‑specific criteria.
b: Pulmonary fibrosis: mild (≤10 % of lung volume), moderate (10‑30 %), severe (>30 %).
Anti‑GBM disease: renal involvement graded by eGFR (≥30 ml/min/1.73 m² mild, 15‑29 moderate, <15 severe).

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, infectious and immune‑mediated processes dominate BM damage.
b: Autoimmune anti‑GBM disease (Goodpasture syndrome).
Infectious pulmonary fibrosis (post‑TB, post‑parasitic).
Chronic exposure to silica or asbestos (occupational).
Malaria‑associated renal microvascular injury.
HIV‑associated collapsing glomerulopathy.

sections.p: Clinical features reflect the organ involved and the degree of barrier disruption.
b: Lung: progressive dyspnoea on exertion, dry cough, hypoxaemia, reduced DLCO.
Kidney: hematuria (microscopic or gross), proteinuria, rising creatinine, oliguria in severe cases.

sections.p: Targeted tests confirm BM pathology and assess functional impact.

t.b: Shows interstitial infiltrates or honey‑comb pattern; thickened BM appears as reticular opacities.
Quantifies diffusion impairment; a low DLCO indicates BM thickening in the alveolar‑capillary membrane.
Detects dysmorphic red cells and protein; suggests glomerular BM injury.
Assesses renal filtration loss; falling eGFR signals worsening BM damage.
Directly visualises BM thickening, immune deposits; guides specific therapy.
Use clinical picture (rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis + pulmonary haemorrhage) to start empiric therapy.

sections.p: Prompt recognition prevents irreversible organ loss.
b: Rapid rise in creatinine >30 % within 48 h.
Severe hypoxaemia (SpO₂ <85 %) despite oxygen.
Pulmonary haemorrhage (hemoptysis with anemia).
Progressive dyspnoea limiting daily activities.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, protect the BM, and support organ function.
b: Anti‑GBM disease: high‑dose IV methylprednisolone, cyclophosphamide, and plasma exchange to remove antibodies.
Pulmonary fibrosis: antifibrotic agents (pirfenidone or nintedanib) where available; otherwise optimise oxygen and treat infections.
TB‑related fibrosis: complete anti‑TB regimen plus steroids if active inflammation persists.
Supportive renal care: avoid nephrotoxins, manage fluid balance, consider dialysis when eGFR <15 ml/min/1.73 m².
Lung: repeat DLCO and imaging every 6‑12 months.
Kidney: monthly creatinine/eGFR, urine protein quantification.
Vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus to reduce secondary infections.
Educate patients on avoiding silica, asbestos, and nephrotoxic drugs.
Pulmonary oedema – both cause dyspnoea but oedema shows rapid fluid shift, crackles, and normal DLCO.
IgA nephropathy – presents with hematuria but lacks anti‑GBM antibodies and BM thickening on biopsy.
Normal chest X‑ray early in pulmonary fibrosis; rely on DLCO and CT if suspicion high.
Negative anti‑GBM ELISA early in disease; repeat if clinical picture fits.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly falling renal function, pulmonary haemorrhage, or severe hypoxaemia requiring high‑flow oxygen.

faq.q: Why does a low DLCO suggest basement membrane disease?
faq.a: DLCO measures gas diffusion across the alveolar‑capillary membrane; thickening of the BM reduces diffusion, lowering DLCO.

faq.q: Can anti‑GBM disease present without lung involvement?
faq.a: Yes; isolated renal anti‑GBM disease occurs, but clinicians should still assess for subclinical pulmonary injury.

faq.q: What is the role of plasma exchange in anti‑GBM disease?
faq.a: It rapidly removes circulating antibodies, limiting further BM damage while immunosuppression takes effect.

exam: A patient with rapidly rising creatinine and hemoptysis – what is the next immediate investigation and why? — Order anti‑GBM antibody test and chest imaging; they confirm Goodpasture syndrome, guiding urgent plasma exchange.
How does thickening of the alveolar‑capillary basement membrane affect DLCO? — It increases diffusion distance, reducing DLCO and causing exertional hypoxaemia.
What distinguishes pulmonary fibrosis from pulmonary oedema on bedside examination? — Fibrosis shows fine bibasal crackles and a low DLCO; oedema shows rapid fluid shift, egophony, and normal DLCO.

Why is cyclophosphamide preferred over azathioprine in acute anti‑GBM disease? — Cyclophosphamide provides stronger immunosuppression needed for rapid antibody suppression; azathioprine is slower acting.
In a low‑resource setting without CT, how would you suspect BM‑related pulmonary fibrosis? — Rely on progressive dyspnoea, reduced DLCO, and characteristic reticular pattern on chest X‑ray.
What are the red‑flag renal values indicating need for dialysis in BM injury? — eGFR <15 ml/min/1.73 m² or creatinine >500 µmol/L with oliguria.
Explain why anti‑GBM antibodies are pathogenic rather than merely a marker. — They bind directly to the glomerular and alveolar BM, activating complement and causing necrotising inflammation.

How would you counsel a patient with occupational silica exposure to prevent BM damage? — Use protective masks, improve ventilation, and undergo regular lung function testing to detect early fibrosis.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: Focused history and a systematic physical exam can identify basement‑membrane (BM) injury in the lung or kidney even when imaging is unavailable.
b: Onset and progression of dyspnoea or cough; ask for exertional limits and orthopnoea.
Hemoptysis – quantity, timing, relation to infection or trauma.
Exposure history: silica, asbestos, farming dust, TB contacts, recent malaria or HIV infection.
Medication and herbal use (e.g., NSAIDs, gold salts, traditional remedies).
Renal symptoms: hematuria (visible or microscopic), proteinuria, oliguria, swelling, flank pain.
Systemic features: fever, weight loss, arthralgia, skin rash, recent pregnancy.
Family history of autoimmune disease (SLE, Goodpasture) or hereditary nephropathies.

t.b: Detects use of accessory muscles, cyanosis, or clubbing; a positive sign suggests chronic hypoxaemia but cannot quantify diffusion impairment.
Fine end‑inspiratory crackles over bases indicate interstitial involvement; they do not differentiate fibrosis from pulmonary oedema.
Dullness may indicate consolidation or pleural effusion; normal resonance does not exclude early interstitial disease.
Pitting oedema suggests volume overload or nephrotic syndrome; its absence does not rule out renal BM injury.
Shifting dullness confirms fluid but cannot tell whether caused by hypoalbuminaemia from nephrotic loss or portal hypertension.
Enlarged kidneys may indicate active inflammation; small kidneys suggest chronic scarring, but size alone is not diagnostic.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Select tests answer specific clinical questions; when a test is unavailable, use the next best alternative and interpret with local disease prevalence in mind.
b: Serum creatinine and eGFR – assess renal filtration; a rise >30 % in 48 h signals acute injury requiring urgent review.
Urinalysis with microscopy – look for dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts, and protein; >3 g/day protein suggests nephrotic range, casts point to glomerular BM damage.
Anti‑GBM antibody ELISA – positive result confirms Goodpasture; a negative result does not exclude other BM diseases.
Chest X‑ray – shows reticular pattern, honey‑comb, or alveolar infiltrates; cannot differentiate fibrosis from oedema without CT.
Point‑of‑care ultrasound (POCUS) lung – B‑lines indicate interstitial fluid; multiple diffuse B‑lines with normal cardiac function favour fibrosis.
GeneXpert MTB/RIF on sputum – first‑line test for active TB; a positive result explains post‑TB fibrosis.
Serum complement C3/C4 – usually normal in anti‑GBM disease; low C3 suggests immune‑complex disease.
Renal biopsy (if feasible) – light microscopy for crescents, immunofluorescence for linear IgG, EM for BM thickness; unavailable → rely on serology and clinical picture.

t.b: Answers: extent of alveolar‑capillary BM thickening; a reduction >20 % of predicted supports interstitial fibrosis, but cannot specify cause.
Helps calculate serum‑ascites albumin gradient if ascites present; gradient >1.1 g/dL indicates portal hypertension, not directly BM injury.
Detects anaemia from chronic disease or haemoptysis; neutrophil <0.5 ×10⁹/L may prompt growth‑factor support during cyclophosphamide.
Quantifies proteinuria when 24‑h collection unavailable; UPCR >3 g/g indicates nephrotic range, guiding immunosuppression intensity.
Quantifies % lung involvement: ≤10 % mild, >10‑30 % moderate, >30 % severe. In low‑resource settings, estimate severity by clinical dyspnoea grade.

sections.p: Combine clinical, serologic and (when possible) histologic data to classify BM disease and decide urgency of therapy.
b: Goodpasture syndrome: hemoptysis + rapidly rising creatinine + positive anti‑GBM antibodies + linear IgG on renal biopsy.
Pulmonary fibrosis secondary to infection or exposure: chronic dyspnoea, HRCT pattern of reticulation, no anti‑GBM antibodies, history of TB, silica or asbestos.
Post‑TB fibrosis: prior microbiologically confirmed TB, persistent radiographic changes, normal anti‑GBM, DLCO reduction.
Renal BM injury staging (anti‑GBM): eGFR ≥30 ml/min/1.73 m² mild; 15‑29 moderate; <15 severe.
Pulmonary fibrosis severity by HRCT % lung involvement: ≤10 % mild, >10‑30 % moderate, >30 % severe.

sections.p: Several diseases mimic BM injury; careful attention to exposure, serology and histology separates them.

t.b: Presents with recurrent hemoptysis and anaemia but no renal involvement and negative anti‑GBM; bronchoalveolar lavage shows hemosiderin‑laden macrophages.
Acute dyspnoea with crackles and B‑lines; BNP elevated, cardiomegaly on X‑ray, rapid response to diuretics distinguishes it from fibrosis.
Renal dysfunction with low complement C3/C4, positive ANA/dsDNA, granular “full‑house” IF pattern; anti‑GBM negative.
Nephrotic proteinuria with spike‑and‑dome EM pattern; anti‑PLA2R antibodies may be present; no pulmonary haemorrhage.
History of silica exposure, nodular upper‑lobe opacities on X‑ray, restrictive spirometry; anti‑GBM negative.

sections.p: A structured ladder guides clinicians from stabilisation to definitive therapy, ensuring organ protection while accounting for resource constraints.
b: 1. Stabilise airway, breathing and circulation; give supplemental O₂ to keep SpO₂ ≥ 90 % and correct severe metabolic acidosis.
2. Obtain urgent serology (anti‑GBM antibodies) and bedside urine microscopy; start high‑dose IV methylprednisolone while awaiting results.
4. Add cyclophosphamide (IV or oral) for induction; switch to azathioprine or mycophenolate for maintenance after remission.
5. For pulmonary fibrosis without anti‑GBM, start antifibrotic therapy where available; otherwise optimise oxygen, pulmonary rehab and treat underlying infection.
6. Monitor renal function (serum creatinine, urine output) and pulmonary status (DLCO, chest X‑ray) daily; adjust immunosuppression if infections emerge.

7. Escalate to renal replacement therapy if creatinine >7 mg/dL, oliguria <400 mL/day with hyperkalaemia or refractory acidosis; refer to tertiary centre for lung transplant evaluation if progressive fibrosis despite therapy.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Key adverse events of the main agents and practical steps to mitigate them, especially where laboratory monitoring is limited.
b: Cyclophosphamide – bone‑marrow suppression, haemorrhagic cystitis, alopecia; obtain CBC twice weekly, hydrate aggressively, give mesna if IV, hold drug if neutrophils <0.5 ×10⁹/L.
Azathioprine – hepatotoxicity, myelosuppression; check liver enzymes weekly, stop if ALT >3 × ULN, monitor CBC, avoid in TPMT deficiency (if testing unavailable, start at low dose and watch counts).
Mycophenolate – diarrhoea, cytopenia; ensure adequate hydration, treat diarrhoea with loperamide, hold if neutrophils <0.5 ×10⁹/L.
Plasma exchange – citrate‑induced hypocalcaemia, line infection; give calcium gluconate prophylactically, use aseptic technique, monitor for bleeding.
Antifibrotics (pirfenidone, nintedanib) – photosensitivity, GI upset, liver enzyme rise; advise sun protection, give anti‑emetics, check ALT/AST monthly.

sections.p: Recognise life‑threatening sequelae that demand rapid escalation or referral.
b: Severe hypoxaemia (SpO₂ <85 % on 15 L O₂) or worsening pulmonary haemorrhage → transfer to ICU, consider additional plasma exchange.
Infection during immunosuppression (fever >38 °C, new infiltrates) → stop cyclophosphamide, start broad‑spectrum antibiotics, reassess need for steroids.
Progressive fibrosis on serial chest X‑ray/ultrasound with DLCO fall >15 % → discuss referral for lung transplant or enrolment in clinical trial.
Thrombotic microangiopathy (schistocytes, platelets <100 ×10⁹/L) → add plasma exchange and consider complement inhibitor if available.

sections.p: Co‑morbidities and local conditions that modify presentation, investigations and therapy.
b: Active TB – GeneXpert positive sputum requires anti‑TB therapy before high‑dose steroids; avoid plasma exchange if uncontrolled sepsis.
Malnutrition – low albumin reduces drug binding; monitor free drug levels where possible, give nutritional support before cyclophosphamide.
Pregnancy – avoid cyclophosphamide; use steroids and plasma exchange; azathioprine is relatively safe for maintenance after first trimester.
Diabetes – steroids exacerbate hyperglycaemia; intensify insulin regimen, check capillary glucose q4h.
Alcohol use – potentiates liver toxicity of azathioprine; counsel abstinence, monitor LFTs.

sections.p: Tailored considerations for vulnerable populations and low‑resource environments.
b: Children – weight‑based dosing of steroids and cyclophosphamide; use plasma exchange only in centres with paediatric expertise; monitor growth parameters.
Pregnancy – prioritize steroids and plasma exchange; defer cyclophosphamide until postpartum; counsel on fetal monitoring.
Elderly – higher risk of steroid‑induced delirium and infection; start with lower steroid dose, use azathioprine for maintenance, watch for cytopenias.
People with HIV – combine antiretroviral therapy with anti‑GBM treatment; prophylactic cotrimoxazole and fluconazole; monitor for drug‑drug interactions (e.g., ritonavir with azathioprine).

Low‑resource settings – use GeneXpert for TB rule‑out, bedside ultrasound for pleural effusion, point‑of‑care creatinine; if plasma exchange unavailable, give high‑dose steroids and consider immunoadsorption if locally feasible.

sections.p: Sample questions covering bedside assessment, interpretation of investigations, management decisions and special‑population nuances.
b: 2. A patient with suspected anti‑GBM disease has normal complement levels. How does this influence your diagnosis? (Answer: it supports but does not confirm; continue work‑up).
3. When anti‑GBM antibodies are unavailable, which renal biopsy finding is diagnostic? (Answer: linear IgG deposition along the glomerular basement membrane).

4. In a malaria‑endemic area, a child presents with haematuria and rising creatinine; what confounder must you consider before starting cyclophosphamide? (Answer: possible concurrent malaria‑induced renal injury).

5. How would you modify the induction regimen for a pregnant woman with Goodpasture syndrome? (Answer: give high‑dose IV methylprednisolone and plasma exchange; defer cyclophosphamide until after delivery).
6. A patient on cyclophosphamide develops neutrophils of 0.4 ×10⁹/L. What is the next step? (Answer: hold cyclophosphamide, give growth‑factor support, monitor CBC).
7. Which laboratory threshold prompts urgent dialysis in anti‑GBM renal disease? (Answer: creatinine >7 mg/dL with oliguria <400 mL/day or refractory metabolic acidosis).
9. What is the primary reason to avoid azathioprine in the acute phase of anti‑GBM disease? (Answer: it is slower acting; cyclophosphamide provides rapid immunosuppression).

10. A patient with silica exposure develops progressive dyspnoea; what preventive advice reduces further basement‑membrane damage? (Answer: cessation of exposure, use of respirators, smoking cessation).

facts: Anti‑GBM disease: linear IgG deposition on glomerular basement membrane by immunofluorescence.
Pulmonary fibrosis staging by HRCT: mild ≤10 % lung involvement, moderate >10‑30 %, severe >30 %.
Anti‑GBM renal severity: eGFR ≥30 ml/min/1.73 m² mild, 15‑29 moderate, <15 severe.
Rapid renal deterioration in anti‑GBM: rise in creatinine >30 % in 48 h with metabolic acidosis or hyperkalaemia warrants plasma exchange.
Goodpasture syndrome treatment induction: high‑dose IV methylprednisolone, cyclophosphamide, and plasma exchange.
First‑line TB test in Kenya: sputum GeneXpert MTB/RIF, not smear microscopy.
DLCO reduction correlates with thickness of alveolar‑capillary basement membrane; >20 % drop suggests significant fibrosis.
Cyclophosphamide bone‑marrow monitoring: CBC twice weekly; consider G‑CSF if neutrophils <0.5 ×10⁹/L.
Normal complement levels are typical but not diagnostic for anti‑GBM disease.

vivas.q: Define anti‑GBM disease and its pathognomonic histology.
vivas.a: Autoimmune attack on type IV collagen of glomerular and alveolar basement membranes; linear IgG staining on immunofluorescence.

vivas.q: What bedside test helps differentiate pulmonary fibrosis from pulmonary oedema?
vivas.a: Fine inspiratory crackles that are bibasal and persist after sitting upright suggest fibrosis; rapid fluid‑wet rales that change with position suggest oedema.

vivas.q: Why is cyclophosphamide preferred over azathioprine for induction in acute anti‑GBM disease?
vivas.a: Cyclophosphamide provides rapid, potent immunosuppression needed to halt antibody production; azathioprine is slower and used for maintenance.

vivas.q: In a low‑resource setting without CT, how would you suspect BM‑related pulmonary fibrosis?
vivas.a: History of progressive dyspnoea, dry cough, reduced DLCO on simple spirometry, and fine bibasal crackles; exclude active infection with GeneXpert.

vivas.q: What are the red‑flag renal values indicating need for dialysis in BM injury?
vivas.a: Creatinine >5 mg/dL, oliguria <400 mL/day, rising creatinine >30 % in 48 h with acidosis or hyperkalaemia.

vivas.q: Explain why anti‑GBM antibodies are pathogenic rather than merely a marker.
vivas.a: They bind directly to type IV collagen, fixing complement and recruiting neutrophils, causing basement membrane rupture and haemorrhage.

vivas.q: How would you counsel a patient with occupational silica exposure to prevent BM damage?
vivas.a: Use water‑spray and respirators, limit exposure time, regular health surveillance with chest X‑ray and renal function tests.

vivas.q: A middle‑aged patient presents with chronic skin lesions and a biopsy shows band‑like lymphohistiocytic infiltrate at the dermo‑epidermal junction with basal vacuolisation. Direct immunofluorescence demonstrates IgG and C3 at the basement membrane. What is the diagnosis?
vivas.a: Lupus erythematosus (discoid or systemic) – interface dermatitis with lupus band test positive.

vivas.q: Renal biopsy shows diffuse GBM thickening with spike‑and‑dome on silver stain. Which pathology underlies this?
vivas.a: Membranous nephropathy – immune complex deposition on the subepithelial side.

vivas.q: A 25‑year‑old woman with malar rash, arthralgia, anti‑dsDNA positivity develops diffuse proliferative GN. What immunofluorescence pattern is expected?
vivas.a: Full‑house pattern: IgG, IgA, IgM, C3 and C1q granular deposits.

vivas.q: Patient with hemoptysis, iron‑deficiency anaemia, normal renal function and negative anti‑GBM antibodies – likely diagnosis?
vivas.a: Idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis – pulmonary bleeding without renal involvement.

vivas.q: Nasal polyp histology shows oedematous stroma, eosinophils, thickened basement membrane and which epithelium?
Acute kidney injury with nephritic sediment and pulmonary haemorrhage; renal biopsy shows linear IgG along GBM. Which diagnosis?
Renal biopsy shows duplicated basement membrane subendothelial on EM. What does this represent?
vivas.a: Organising (healing) phase of membranoproliferative GN – “tram‑track” appearance.

vivas.q: Low C3 with normal C1q and C4 and EM dense ribbon‑like deposits – which disease?
Key differences between idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis and Goodpasture syndrome?
vivas.a: IPH lacks renal disease and anti‑GBM antibodies; Goodpasture has both lung and renal involvement with circulating anti‑GBM antibodies.

mcqs.q: A 30‑year‑old man with rapidly rising creatinine (35 % in 48 h) and hemoptysis. Which is the most appropriate immediate therapy?
o: Plasma exchange plus cyclophosphamide and steroids
mcqs.e: Plasma exchange removes pathogenic antibodies; combined with cyclophosphamide and steroids for induction.

mcqs.q: Which test best quantifies the functional impact of alveolar‑capillary basement membrane thickening?
mcqs.e: DLCO directly reflects gas transfer across the alveolar‑capillary membrane.

mcqs.q: In a patient with suspected membranous nephropathy, which biopsy finding is diagnostic?
mcqs.e: Spike‑and‑dome pattern reflects epithelial reaction to subepithelial immune deposits.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical feature of Goodpasture syndrome?
mcqs.e: Granular IgA deposits are not seen; Goodpasture shows linear IgG.

mcqs.q: A patient with chronic cough, dyspnoea, and HRCT showing 25 % lung involvement. What stage of pulmonary fibrosis is this?
Which bedside maneuver helps differentiate pleural effusion from pulmonary fibrosis?
mcqs.e: Dullness on percussion suggests fluid; fibrosis usually yields resonant percussion.

cases.v: A 28‑year‑old male farmer presents with 3 months of progressive dyspnoea on exertion, dry cough, and recent haemoptysis. He reports recent silica dust exposure. SpO₂ 88 % on room air, fine bibasal crackles, and creatinine 1.2 mg/dL. GeneXpert negative. Chest X‑ray shows reticular infiltrates.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a: Silica‑related pulmonary fibrosis with possible anti‑GBM overlap; however, absence of renal dysfunction makes isolated silica fibrosis most likely.

qs.q: Which investigation would confirm basement membrane involvement?
qs.a: DLCO measurement (marked reduction) and, if available, HRCT quantifying fibrosis; renal biopsy is not indicated without renal impairment.

qs.q: Outline the initial management steps in this low‑resource setting.
qs.a: Stop further silica exposure, provide supplemental oxygen, start oral corticosteroids if rapid progression, consider referral for antifibrotic therapy if available; monitor renal function and DLCO.

cases.v: A 45‑year‑old woman presents with sudden onset haemoptysis, anaemia (Hb 8 g/dL), and rising creatinine from 1.0 to 1.8 mg/dL over 24 h. Anti‑GBM antibodies are positive. Chest X‑ray shows diffuse alveolar infiltrates.

qs.a: Anti‑GBM disease (Goodpasture syndrome) with pulmonary‑renal involvement.

qs.q: What is the first‑line treatment regimen?
qs.a: Plasma exchange daily (or every other day) plus high‑dose IV methylprednisolone and cyclophosphamide.

qs.q: What red‑flag indicates need for emergent dialysis?
qs.a: Creatinine >5 mg/dL, oliguria <400 mL/day, or rising creatinine >30 % in 48 h with metabolic acidosis or hyperkalaemia.

mistakes: Confusing sputum smear microscopy with GeneXpert as the first TB test in Kenya.
Using a 30 % creatinine rise alone to trigger plasma exchange without accompanying acidosis or hyperkalaemia.
Stating crackles are specific for interstitial fibrosis; they also occur in pulmonary oedema.
Claiming normal complement levels definitively diagnose anti‑GBM disease.
Mis‑staging pulmonary fibrosis by placing 30 % involvement in both moderate and severe categories.
Suggesting azathioprine replaces cyclophosphamide in acute anti‑GBM induction.
Starting growth‑factor support for neutrophils <1.0 ×10⁹/L instead of the correct <0.5 ×10⁹/L threshold.
Initiating dialysis solely on oliguria without considering hyperkalaemia, acidosis, or creatinine level.
exam: Define anti‑GBM disease and its pathognomonic histology. — Autoimmune attack on type IV collagen of glomerular and alveolar basement membranes; linear IgG staining on immunofluorescence.

What bedside test helps differentiate pulmonary fibrosis from pulmonary oedema? — Fine inspiratory crackles that are bibasal and persist after sitting upright suggest fibrosis; rapid fluid‑wet rales that change with position suggest oedema.

Why is cyclophosphamide preferred over azathioprine for induction in acute anti‑GBM disease? — Cyclophosphamide provides rapid, potent immunosuppression needed to halt antibody production; azathioprine is slower and used for maintenance.

In a low‑resource setting without CT, how would you suspect BM‑related pulmonary fibrosis? — History of progressive dyspnoea, dry cough, reduced DLCO on simple spirometry, and fine bibasal crackles; exclude active infection with GeneXpert.
What are the red‑flag renal values indicating need for dialysis in BM injury? — Creatinine >5 mg/dL, oliguria <400 mL/day, rising creatinine >30 % in 48 h with acidosis or hyperkalaemia.

Explain why anti‑GBM antibodies are pathogenic rather than merely a marker. — They bind directly to type IV collagen, fixing complement and recruiting neutrophils, causing basement membrane rupture and haemorrhage.

How would you counsel a patient with occupational silica exposure to prevent BM damage? — Use water‑spray and respirators, limit exposure time, regular health surveillance with chest X‑ray and renal function tests.

A middle‑aged patient presents with chronic skin lesions and a biopsy shows band‑like lymphohistiocytic infiltrate at the dermo‑epidermal junction with basal vacuolisation. Direct immunofluorescence demonstrates IgG and C3 at the basement membrane. What is the diagnosis? — Lupus erythematosus (discoid or systemic) – interface dermatitis with lupus band test positive.
Renal biopsy shows diffuse GBM thickening with spike‑and‑dome on silver stain. Which pathology underlies this? — Membranous nephropathy – immune complex deposition on the subepithelial side.

A 25‑year‑old woman with malar rash, arthralgia, anti‑dsDNA positivity develops diffuse proliferative GN. What immunofluorescence pattern is expected? — Full‑house pattern: IgG, IgA, IgM, C3 and C1q granular deposits.

Patient with hemoptysis, iron‑deficiency anaemia, normal renal function and negative anti‑GBM antibodies – likely diagnosis? — Idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis – pulmonary bleeding without renal involvement.
Nasal polyp histology shows oedematous stroma, eosinophils, thickened basement membrane and which epithelium? — Respiratory (pseudostratified ciliated) epithelium.
Acute kidney injury with nephritic sediment and pulmonary haemorrhage; renal biopsy shows linear IgG along GBM. Which diagnosis? — Goodpasture syndrome (anti‑GBM disease).
Renal biopsy shows duplicated basement membrane subendothelial on EM. What does this represent? — Organising (healing) phase of membranoproliferative GN – “tram‑track” appearance.
